problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-2y).
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=6x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$

feedback.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x+2y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=4y-C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2(2x+y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{2z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4z+1}{2z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2z}{4z+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{2z}{4z+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{1}{4z+1})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}(z-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|4z+1|) & =x+K \\ 4z-\operatorname{ln}⁡|4z+1| & =8x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=8K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x+4y-\operatorname{ln}⁡|8x+4y+1| & =8x+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|8x+4y+1| & =4y-C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=8x+4y+1.
$$
